content.text:
Annual Review reporting for programme code MWI-EDU-AR-4471 covered the period 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025, with the review pack due to FCDO by 21 November 2025. The funded programme ran from 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2026, with an approved FCDO contribution of GBP 1,240,000. Year 1 delivery remained broadly on track against plan, although performance and finance records were not fully aligned to the award-letter review window in all partner returns. Headline output results were mixed but generally positive. OP1.1 exceeded target, with 684 girls re-enrolled or retained against a Year 1 target of 650. OP1.3 also exceeded target, with 438 girls completing remedial sessions against a target of 420. OP2.1 surpassed its milestone, delivering 31 functional girls' latrine stances against a target of 24. OP3.2 slightly exceeded plan, reaching 571 girls with re-entry kits against a target of 550. OP4.3 also performed above target, training 136 school and community actors on re-entry and safeguarding against a target of 120. A smaller group of indicators fell short of Year 1 targets and explained the main areas requiring management attention. Attendance at or above eighty per cent reached 472 girls against a target of 500. Caregiver hardship grants reached 392 caregivers against a target of 400. Schools with menstrual health supplies and trained teachers reached 17 against a target of 20, and district learning meetings reached three against a target of four. The main recorded reason for the OP2.2 shortfall was delay in menstrual health supplies, while late attendance registers from four schools affected OP1.2 reporting completeness. Performance against the stated outcome was positive overall. The programme outcome aimed for adolescent girls to demonstrate improved school retention, attendance and learning continuity with reduced barriers [fact:objectives.out1_improved_retention_attendance]. Year 1 monitoring reported that supported girls’ attendance and retention improved against Year 1 milestones, using term attendance registers and school safeguarding pathway checks, with variance notes recorded in the AR1 export [gap:performance_and_conclusions:table:outcome_assessment].

Progress against expected results was mixed but broadly on track. Re-enrolment or retention reached 684 girls against a Year 1 target of 650, and remedial sessions reached 438 girls against a target of 420 [fact:indicators.op1_1_girls_reenrolled_retained.y1_actual][fact:indicators.op1_1_girls_reenrolled_retained.y1_target][fact:indicators.op1_3_girls_remedial_sessions.y1_actual][fact:indicators.op1_3_girls_remedial_sessions.y1_target]. Attendance at 80% or more of school days reached 472 girls against a target of 500, so this indicator fell short [fact:indicators.op1_2_girls_attending_80pct.y1_actual][fact:indicators.op1_2_girls_attending_80pct.y1_target]. The available explanation was that four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations].

Infrastructure and school environment results were also uneven. Functional girls’ latrine stances reached 31 against a Year 1 target of 24, exceeding plan [fact:indicators.op2_1_latrine_stances_functional.y1_actual][fact:indicators.op2_1_latrine_stances_functional.y1_target]. By contrast, schools with menstrual health supplies and trained teachers reached 17 against a target of 20 [fact:indicators.op2_2_schools_menstrual_health.y1_actual][fact:indicators.op2_2_schools_menstrual_health.y1_target]. Submitted records attributed this variance to menstrual health supply delays, and programme assumptions on focal teacher availability held in most schools but not all, as three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks][gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:realised_assumptions]. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, and Year 1 monitoring did not report any major incident trend [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:safeguarding_risk_where_relevant].

Economic support outputs were close to plan overall. Hardship grants reached 392 caregivers against a target of 400, while re-entry kits reached 571 girls against a target of 550 [fact:indicators.op3_1_caregivers_hardship_grant.y1_actual][fact:indicators.op3_1_caregivers_hardship_grant.y1_target][fact:indicators.op3_2_girls_reentry_kit.y1_actual][fact:indicators.op3_2_girls_reentry_kit.y1_target]. Follow-up for hardship households reached a proportion of 0.68 in Year 1; the proposal endline target for this measure was 85%, but no Year 1 target fact was available in the submitted facts set, so only partial assessment was possible here [fact:indicators.op3_3_hardship_households_followup.y1_actual][fact:indicators.op3_3_hardship_households_followup.proposal_endline_target]. Controls over transfer lists appear to have worked as intended during the period, with no evidence that funds were used other than intended; deduplication removed 16 caregiver records before payment [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:funds_not_used_as_intended_risk].

System strengthening outputs showed reasonable delivery with some slippage. District learning meetings reached 3 against a Year 1 target of 4 [fact:indicators.op4_1_district_learning_meetings.y1_actual][fact:indicators.op4_1_district_learning_meetings.y1_target]. Training on re-entry and safeguarding reached 136 school and community actors against a target of 120, exceeding plan [fact:indicators.op4_3_actors_trained_reentry.y1_actual][fact:indicators.op4_3_actors_trained_reentry.y1_target]. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, although late register submission from four schools affected attendance reporting quality [gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:partner_performance].

The evidence base was adequate for an Annual Review but had limits. Indicator actuals were drawn from the BridgeLight AR1 export with source notes per output, and supporting evidence included school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists, and district validation samples [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evidence_base_strength][gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:new_evidence]. No standalone external evaluation was commissioned in Year 1; monitoring relied on termly indicator returns and partner spot checks [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evaluation_progress]. There was also a reporting-period inconsistency in submitted records: partner returns used 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25 while the award letter set the first Annual Review period at 2024-10-15 to 2025-10-14, with the review pack due by 2025-11-21 [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations][fact:reporting.annual_review_period_1.start][fact:reporting.annual_review_period_0.end][fact not available][fact not available]

A smaller set of indicators fell short of Year 1 milestones and explained the lower proposed scores on those rows. OP1.2 recorded 472 girls attending at least 80% of school days against a target of 500. Submitted records stated that four schools sent attendance registers late, which affected attendance reporting [fact:indicators.op1_2_girls_attending_80pct.y1_actual, fact:indicators.op1_2_girls_attending_80pct.y1_target, gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations]. OP2.2 reached 17 schools with menstrual health supplies and trained teachers against a target of 20. OP3.1 reached 392 caregivers receiving a hardship grant against a target of 400, while OP3.3 recorded follow-up for 0.68 of hardship households against a Year 1 milestone that was stated as 75% in proposal records [fact:indicators.op3_1_caregivers_hardship_grant.y1_actual, fact:indicators.op3_1_caregivers_hardship_grant.y1_target, fact:indicators.op3_3_hardship_households_followup.y1_actual, fact:indicators.op3_3_hardship_households_followup.proposal_endline_target]. OP4.1 also under-delivered slightly, with 3 district learning meetings held against a target of 4 [fact:indicators.op4_1_district_learning_meetings.y1_actual, fact:indicators.op4_1_district_learning_meetings.y1_target].

The evidence base for scoring drew on school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists and district validation samples [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:new_evidence]. No standalone external evaluation was commissioned in Year 0; monitoring relied on termly indicator returns and partner spot checks [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evaluation_progress].

content.text:
During the first Annual Review period, from 2024-10-15 to 2025-10-14, no new material risks were reported beyond those already recorded in the grant risk register. The main issue that affected delivery was delay in menstrual health supplies, which contributed to OP2.2 reaching 17 schools against a Year 1 target of 20. This was a contained delivery risk rather than a wider programme disruption. [fact:reporting.annual_review_period_1.start][fact:reporting.annual_review_period_1.end][gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks][fact:indicators.op2_2_schools_menstrual_health.y1_actual][fact:indicators.op2_2_schools_menstrual_health.y1_target]

A key implementation assumption held in most schools: community focal teachers were available to support delivery. However, this did not hold everywhere. Three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training, which helps explain the shortfall on OP2.2 and points to a specific staffing constraint rather than a failure across the whole approach. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:realised_assumptions][fact:indicators.op2_2_schools_menstrual_health.y1_actual][fact:indicators.op2_2_schools_menstrual_health.y1_target]

Climate and environmental factors did not stop delivery in Year 1. Monitoring reported increased lake-shore transport costs for OP1.1, but no major climate shock halted implementation. Despite that pressure, OP1.1 still exceeded its Year 1 target, with 684 girls re-enrolled or retained against a target of 650. This suggests that cost pressure was managed without loss of core output delivery, although it may have contributed to budget variance on that line, where actual spend was GBP 174,850 against a budget of GBP 162,000. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:climate_environment_risk][fact:indicators.op1_1_girls_reenrolled_retained.y1_actual][fact:indicators.op1_1_girls_reenrolled_retained.y1_target][fact:financials.lines.op1_1.y1_actual][fact:financials.lines.op1_1.y1_budget]

On fiduciary control, submitted records reported no evidence that funds were used other than as intended. For hardship grants, 16 caregiver records were deduplicated before payment, which shows that payment controls identified and removed duplicate entries before disbursement. That control was relevant given the scale of OP3.1 delivery, where 392 caregivers received hardship grants during Year 1 against a target of 400. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:funds_not_used_as_intended_risk][fact:indicators.op3_1_caregivers_hardship_grant.y1_actual][fact:indicators.op3_1_caregivers_hardship_grant.y1_target]

Safeguarding controls remained active during the period. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, and Year 1 monitoring returns did not report any major incident trend. This indicates that referral arrangements were functioning at least at a basic operational level during implementation. The records available for this section did not provide incident counts or case disaggregation, so assurance is based on monitoring returns rather than detailed safeguarding case analysis. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:safeguarding_risk_where_relevant]

Control issues in monitoring data also affected risk management quality. Partner returns used a review period of 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25, while the award letter set the first Annual Review period as 2024-10-15 to 2025-10-14; finance had not recut the reporting window at the time of review. In addition, four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting. These were data quality and reporting control weaknesses rather than indications of misuse of funds, but they reduced precision in performance tracking and should be treated as management issues requiring follow-up. [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations][fact:reporting.annual_review_period_1.start][fact:reporting.annual_review_period_1.end]

Overall, risks were managed with mixed but adequate control performance during the period under review. Delivery continued without major climate or safeguarding disruption; fiduciary checks identified duplicate hardship grant records before payment; and the main materialised programme risk was supply delay affecting menstrual health support in a limited number of schools. The main control gaps were reporting-period misalignment and late attendance records, both of which weakened assurance over some indicator reporting even where implementation remained broadly on track. Value for money in Year 1 was mixed but acceptable overall, with stronger evidence on effectiveness and efficiency than on economy and equity. Total Year 1 actual spend was GBP 920,420 against a Year 1 budget of GBP 880,000, so expenditure ran above plan during the period. This variance needs to be read alongside a reporting-period limitation: partner returns used 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25, while the award letter set the first Annual Review period as 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025, and finance had not recut the figures at the time of reporting. [fact:financials.y1_actual.total; fact:financials.y1_budget.total; fact:reporting.annual_review_period_1.start; fact:reporting.annual_review_period_1.end; gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations]

On economy, spending pressure appeared in several output lines. OP1.1 spent GBP 174,850 against a budget of GBP 162,000, and lake-shore transport costs increased on that line during Year 1. OP2.1 spent GBP 148,900 against GBP 121,000. OP3.2 spent GBP 109,250 against GBP 103,000, and OP4.3 spent GBP 58,630 against GBP 54,000. At the same time, some lines underspent: OP1.3 spent GBP 81,330 against GBP 88,000; OP2.2 spent GBP 39,600 against GBP 42,000; OP3.3 spent GBP 24,980 against GBP 31,000; and OP4.1 spent GBP 32,700 against GBP 39,000. The available evidence therefore suggested active delivery rather than broad cost containment across all lines. There was no evidence that funds were used other than as intended, and hardship grant records were deduplicated before payment by removing 16 caregiver records that risked duplication. On efficiency, delivery converted spend into results reasonably well across most outputs. Several indicators met or exceeded Year 1 targets despite cost pressure in some lines: girls re-enrolled or retained reached 684 against a target of 650; girls completing remedial sessions reached 438 against 420; functional girls' latrine stances reached 31 against 24; girls receiving re-entry kits reached 571 against 550; and school and community actors trained on re-entry and safeguarding reached 136 against 120. Attendance at or above eighty per cent reached only 472 against a target of five hundred, and district learning meetings reached three against four. Menstrual health coverage also fell short at seventeen schools against a target of twenty. The records explained part of this variance through late attendance registers from four schools and menstrual health supply delays affecting OP2.2. content.text:
Recommendations from this review focused on three issues that affected Year 1 performance and reporting quality. First, the review identified the need to recut finance and reporting to the FCDO Annual Review window of 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025, as partner returns were still labelled to a different cycle. Second, menstrual health training needed completion in the three remaining schools where a female focal teacher was not available, which contributed to OP2.2 reaching 17 schools against a target of 20. Third, late attendance registers from four schools needed follow-up because they affected reporting on OP1.2 attendance performance. Priority actions were to close the OP2.2 gap at 17 of 20 schools, complete disposal bins at four latrine units, and align reporting period labelling with the award letter. These actions responded directly to delivery variance and data quality issues recorded during Year 1 rather than adding new workstreams.
